items.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000
items.q: I had to play Duke Ellington and Fats Waller and Fletcher Henderson. These are my people.

ctx.x: Did you have aspirations to become a professional classical pianist?

Yes. And at some point I did. When I was sixteen years old I made a promise to myself to become a concert pianist. I didn’t know that I was going to go to the Korean War. I didn’t know I was going to get in the Army. That kind of changed things. And then when I came out of the Army I went to Juilliard. And the time I spent in Juilliard let me know that it wasn’t the music of Chopin and Brahms and Beethoven that I had to play, it was the music of my people. I had to play Duke Ellington and Fats Waller and Fletcher…

like an awakening to me. I like to call it an epiphany because when I was young, nobody ever talked to me about that kind of stuff. And then I became aware of all of these great people. I mean Willie “The Lion” Smith was a great pianist, Lucky Roberts was a great pianist, Scott Joplin was a great composer, Jelly Roll Morton was a great composer. These people, they meant something. And all of that now, a hundred years later, is meaning something to everybody in the United States. Young people who don’t get that…
